question: Explain database normalization and the goals of 1NF 2NF and 3NF.
expected_concepts: redundancy reduction|update anomalies|1NF atomic values|2NF partial dependency|3NF transitive dependency
reference_context: Normalization structures relational tables to reduce data redundancy and prevent insert, update, and delete anomalies. 1NF enforces atomic cell values and eliminates repeating groups. 2NF builds on 1NF by removing partial dependencies on composite primary keys. 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies so non-key attributes depend only on the primary key.
answer_text: Database normalization organizes relational tables to reduce data redundancy and prevent insert, update, and delete anomalies. First Normal Form (1NF) requires every column to store atomic values with no repeating groups. Second Normal Form (2NF) removes partial dependencies so every non-key attribute depends on the full composite primary key. Third Normal Form (3NF) goes further by eliminating transitive dependencies, ensuring non-key columns depend strictly on the primary key and not on other non-key attributes.

question: What are the four Coffman conditions required for deadlock and how can an OS prevent deadlock?
expected_concepts: mutual exclusion|hold and wait|no preemption|circular wait|lock ordering
reference_context: Deadlock occurs only when four Coffman conditions hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. An operating system prevents deadlock by breaking at least one condition, most practically breaking circular wait by enforcing a strict global lock acquisition ordering or breaking hold and wait by requiring processes to request all needed resources upfront.
answer_text: Deadlock requires four Coffman conditions to hold at the same time: mutual exclusion on non-shareable resources, hold and wait where a process holds one resource while waiting for another, no preemption of held resources, and circular wait forming a cycle of waiting processes. Operating systems prevent deadlock by invalidating at least one condition—most commonly preventing circular wait through a strict global lock ordering, or avoiding hold and wait by acquiring all required locks atomically.

question: Explain the difference between composition and inheritance in OOP and when you prefer composition.
expected_concepts: is-a vs has-a|tight coupling|fragile base class|runtime flexibility|dependency injection
reference_context: Inheritance models an is-a relationship and reuses behavior via subclassing, which can create tight coupling and the fragile base class problem when parent internals change. Composition models a has-a relationship by assembling small collaborating objects (often via dependency injection), providing looser coupling, easier unit testing, and runtime flexibility to swap behaviors.
answer_text: Inheritance models an is-a hierarchy by extending a base class, which can introduce tight coupling and the fragile base class problem whenever superclass changes break subclasses. Composition models a has-a relationship by delegating behavior to injected collaborator objects. I prefer composition when combining independent behaviors or mocking dependencies in tests, because dependency injection gives loose coupling and lets you swap implementations at runtime without deep class hierarchies.
